But once team culture has formed, everyone consciously acts according to shared values, and behavior is proactive.

Culture takes a long time to form, and the team manager is the key to its formation. Carry it through consistently — “what you keep constantly in mind will surely find an echo”.

Above is my overall explanation of the five key dimensions of testing team management. Friends interested in the details can also follow the management section of my systematic testing-skills improvement course, which contains a detailed analysis of these five dimensions and their implementation. Reply outline to view the detailed course catalog.

item.title: Should Testers Provide Test Cases for Developers' Self-Testing?
item.description:
Background

I have received a good number of inquiries asking whether, as a tester, one should provide test cases or test data when developers carry out self-testing.

This is a real dilemma that people often encounter in actual work, especially as many teams now emphasize shift-left testing, making it quite common to require testers to provide cases and prepare test data. At the same time, some teams still use defects as a KPI metric, and this gives rise to a host of side effects:

  1. Problems found during the development phase using the cases provided by testers will inevitably reduce the output of problems found during the testing phase.
  2. If testers provide the cases and problems appear later, is that a development omission or a testing omission?
  3. Once testers have handed the cases to developers, is it still necessary to run the same cases again during the testing phase?
  4. What is the value of testers? Is it simply to write as thorough a set of cases as possible?

The Responsibility of Testing and the Role of Test Cases

In a previous article【】we discussed the true purpose of testing in detail.

So we should be clear: the responsibility of testing is not actually to find bugs, but to reflect the product’s quality status.

In testing work, the main role of test cases is, in fact, to help us sort out and summarize the various test paths before testing begins, and to arrange in advance, according to the product requirements, the key points that need to be tested, so as to avoid omissions during actual execution.

All of the above is the basis for discussing the handover of test cases when we talk about shift-left testing.

Should Test Cases Be Handed Over to Developers?

From the team’s perspective, the ultimate concern must be product quality. According to the well-known defect-cost relationship curve, the earlier a defect is found, the lower the cost, and the stronger the confidence in delivery quality.

So from this angle, shift-left testing—including providing test cases to developers—is consistent with the quality goal.

But in actual practice, a team’s KPI orientation affects how things actually turn out.

That is, if a team takes the number of bugs as its KPI, as many do, then the effect of handing over test cases will inevitably be greatly diminished.

This KPI artificially splits the output of the development team and the testing team: developers need to produce as few bugs as possible, while testers need to find as many bugs as possible.

Test cases and test data actually reflect the testing mindset behind finding bugs. Handing the cases to developers will help them reduce bugs, but it will affect the testers’ own output of found bugs.

So under this orientation, even if testers do provide cases, it is hard to guarantee the coverage of those cases—it only becomes a matter of form.

From the standpoint of product quality, then, as a testing role, it is the duty of the job to provide test cases during the development phase and help the development team complete thorough self-testing—but for this to be truly implemented and to produce results, the prerequisite is that this metric of evaluating by bug count must be abolished.

How Should Omissions Not Covered by Cases Be Defined?

First, we must recognize one fact: it is impossible for testing to achieve 100% full coverage. In the early stages of a project, test cases written on the basis of requirements and a development build that is not yet fully complete can cover an even more limited set of test scenarios.

In actual work, even in system testing, the proportion of bugs found by executing test cases is extremely limited compared with the bugs discovered through exploration in real testing. This is precisely the starting point for promoting exploratory testing.

In other words, in the development phase, after testing has been done according to the cases, it is a 100% certainty that the subsequent system testing phase will go on to find problems that were not covered.

So how can we ensure adequate case coverage at this stage?

First, it must be emphasized once again that quality is a team goal. There is no need to agonize over defining whether it is a development omission or a testing omission—the shared goal is to reduce omissions.

Second, test cases should be viewed as the output of a thinking tool and an embodiment of testing ideas. The cases provided by testers are not necessarily the whole story; developers should likewise think about which scenarios to cover.

The requirement coverage and code coverage of the test cases are relatively suitable quantitative metrics for measuring how well cases cover this stage.

The principle for completing self-testing in the development phase is to ensure that the product’s requirements are fully implemented, that no serious blocking problems arise, and that the product’s main logic and architecture are verified.

Once the goals above have been reached, the development self-testing phase can be considered successfully completed. There is no need to dwell on whether a specific bug was covered during the self-testing phase.

Should the Same Set of Cases Still Be Used in the Testing Phase?

For a product that has undergone thorough self-testing, the test cases that have already been executed in principle do not need to be tested again after the product is submitted for testing. That is, by default, scenarios that have already been verified will not produce problems.

In actual work, however, is the developers’ self-testing thorough? Is case execution rigorous? Is there any gray area in the coverage of the cases themselves? All of these are unknowns.

The tester’s job is to prepare and assess the product’s quality status before it is released. It is hard to say that the parts already self-tested by development need no further assessment.

Therefore, even if the cases themselves have not changed, the same set of cases still needs to be re-verified. Of course, this is a very suitable place to use automated testing to cover the existing cases, so that testers can devote more of their energy to exploratory testing.

Is the Main Value of Testers Producing Test Cases?

From the description above, we can also see that, in the testing phase, a more important responsibility of testers is to complete exploratory testing. Test cases themselves are more of an embodiment of testing thinking and a form of expressing testing ideas; they are only an auxiliary output, not the core of testing.

For testing, as I have mentioned many times in my previous articles, James Bach has a famous paper discussing the difference between testing and checking. Executing according to cases is merely checking and cannot count as testing. Real testing, beyond checking, also includes many abilities such as experimentation, research, exploration, questioning, observation, and reasoning—these are the true abilities that help us uncover deeper product defects and expose product quality problems.

So the value of testers is of course not limited to producing cases. It lies much more in revealing the unknown and in assessing the quality status of a product that is still a black box to the team.

item.title: The 5P Method for Effective Meetings - Stop Meetings from Stealing Your Time
item.description:
Introduction

“Every day is packed with endless meetings! More than half the time is spent listening to a few people arguing!” “They love pulling a huge crowd into every meeting, yet hardly anyone actually speaks up!” “A single requirement change, and a meeting planned for 10 minutes drags on for two hours!”

In fast-paced software development, meetings are an indispensable part of information sharing, decision making, and problem solving. Yet what we often experience is how inefficient they are! According to statistics, a software engineer spends an average of 12 hours per week in various meetings, but 60% of those meetings are proven to be inefficient or even useless .

How can we make meetings a genuine collaboration tool rather than a time sink? In this article, by introducing the 5P method for effective meetings, we will break down the core logic of making meetings more efficient and escape the “sea of meetings”!

What Is the 5P Method?

The 5P method for meetings is essentially the five main aspects we need to focus on when holding a meeting. Handle these five aspects well, and meetings will not sink into the mire of being aimless, lengthy, and inefficient.

People - Who Should Attend?

Case - In a requirements clarification meeting, only the product manager and a few core developers took part, while testers and UI/UX designers were absent. As a result, during development it was discovered that the understanding of the requirements did not match testing expectations, and the UI/UX design also deviated from the implemented features, leading to a large amount of rework later.

One of the most common problems with inefficient meetings is that “the people who should be there aren’t, while a crowd of people who shouldn’t be are.” So making sure all key and necessary stakeholders are invited, while avoiding the participation of irrelevant people, is the first step to a successful meeting.

Focus on the following points:

  • Necessity: Only invite those who can provide key information, participate in decisions, or are directly affected by the meeting outcomes.
  • Representation: If the team is large, invite representatives from each function to attend.
  • Clear roles: Clarify each person’s speaking priorities and responsibilities.

For example, in the requirements clarification meeting above, we can identify the following People roles to attend:

  • Product Owner: Explain the requirements background, user stories, and business value.
  • Development Team Lead/Members: Ask questions from a technical implementation perspective and assess feasibility.
  • Test Lead/QA Engineer: Ask questions from a testability perspective and think through test scenarios.
  • UI/UX Designer: Clarify the details of user interaction and interface design.
  • (Optional) Architect: If the requirements involve complex system architecture changes.

Purpose - Why Are We Holding This Meeting?

Case - An agile retrospective turned into a “gripe session” or a “praise session”; everyone chimed in, but nobody focused on how to improve the workflow and collaboration for the next iteration. The meeting was held, yet by the next iteration the existing problems still had not improved.

A meeting without a goal is like a lone boat at sea that has lost its navigation; it easily loses its bearing, with no guarantee of where it will end up, and ultimately fizzles out.

Only when every participant understands the meeting’s purpose can everyone’s understanding be aligned and the discussion be kept from drifting off the main topic.

And when setting the goal here, a few things should be kept in mind:

  • Goals should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART principle).
  • Try to focus a single meeting on 1-2 core goals, avoiding too many topics that cause loss of focus.
  • Make sure all participants share a common understanding of the meeting goals.

For example, for the iteration retrospective above, we can make the goals explicit:

  • Primary goal: Review what went well and what had problems in the previous iteration, and define concrete improvement measures for the next iteration.
  • Specific sub-goals:
    • Identify the 1-2 obstacles that most affect team efficiency and work out solutions;
    • Identify one good practice that should be maintained.

Process - How Should the Meeting Be Run?

Case - A test case review meeting. Only after the meeting started did everyone receive a thick stack of printed test cases, reading them one by one and raising questions on the spot. The presenter’s explanation lacked focus, and reviewers’ thoughts wandered, causing the meeting to run seriously overtime with extremely poor review results.

If Purpose is about keeping the right heading, then Process is the nautical chart for the ship of the meeting. A clear process guides the meeting in an orderly way, ensures every topic is fully discussed, and reaches the goals within the scheduled time.

This includes agreements on the agenda, time allocation, discussion rules, decision-making methods, and so on.

Using the case above again, we can agree on the Process before the meeting:

  • Structured agenda:
    1. Pre-meeting preparation (5-10 minutes, or completed before the meeting): The host briefly states the review scope, goals, and case background. Emphasize that the test cases have been shared in advance and that participants are assumed to have read them beforehand.
    2. Discussion of key/doubtful cases (30-40 minutes): Focus the discussion on questions collected in advance or cases flagged as important. Set a time limit for discussing each complex case.
    3. Summary and confirmation (10-15 minutes): Consolidate review comments, clarify who is responsible for changes and the deadlines. Confirm whether consensus has been reached on test coverage.
  • Clear discussion rules: For example, encourage constructive opinions, avoid interrupting speakers, and define how to decide when opinions differ (such as majority rule, or a final decision by a specific role).
  • Time control: Set an estimated time for each agenda item and enforce it strictly.

Product - What Are the Outcomes of the Meeting?

Case - A release planning meeting. During the meeting, everyone discussed many feature ideas and potential risks for the new version, but no clear release scope, priorities, or owners were established. After the meeting, people were still vague about “which features the new version should actually include.”

First, let us clear up a misconception: a meeting does not count as having produced output simply because it is over and meeting minutes have been generated. The real outcome of a meeting should be a consensus that can be translated into next actions, and one that is traceable. It can be a decision, an action plan, a solution, a record of consensus, updated documents, and so on. Without a clear deliverable, the meeting is effectively a waste.

For the case above, clear deliverables could be:

  • Confirmed release scope: A clear Features List or set of User Stories, with priorities distinguished.
  • Preliminary timeline: Key milestones and the estimated release date.
  • Clear division of responsibilities: An owner for each major module or task.
  • Identified risks and responses: Document potential risks and initial mitigation plans.
  • Meeting minutes: Include all of the above and specify follow-up items. It is the written record of the meeting outcomes

Pitfall - What Risks Are Anticipated?

Pitfall refers to “what potential problems or obstacles might arise during the meeting, and how do we prevent or respond to them?”

Common Meeting Risks and How to Address Them

  • Topics sprawl and the discussion goes off track:

    • Pitfall: Participants may dig too deeply into a certain detail or bring in unrelated topics.
    • Response (combining Purpose & Process): The host should keep the meeting’s core goal in mind at all times and gently steer the discussion back on track. A “Parking Lot” mechanism can be set up to note points that come up on the spur of the moment but are unrelated to the current topic, to be discussed after the meeting.

  • Key people absent or late:

    • Pitfall: Core decision makers or information providers fail to join on time, so the meeting cannot move forward effectively.
    • Response (combining People): Confirm the time with key people in advance and send meeting reminders. If someone is absent at the last minute, assess whether to continue, adjust the agenda, or reschedule the meeting.

  • A few people dominate the conversation while others stay silent:

    • Pitfall: This can lead to incomplete information and biased decisions.
    • Response (combining Process): The host should consciously invite silent participants to speak, or use methods such as round-robin speaking and anonymous opinion collection to ensure everyone has a chance to contribute.

  • Insufficient preparation and information asymmetry:

    • Pitfall: Participants have not read the materials in advance, so a lot of time in the meeting is spent syncing basic information.
    • Response (combining Purpose & Product): Send meeting materials (such as requirements documents, design drafts, and cases to be reviewed) clearly to participants in advance, and explicitly ask them to read and prepare before the meeting.

  • No clear action plan or follow-up:

    • Pitfall: The discussion is lively, but nothing is translated into concrete actions, and it ultimately fizzles out.
    • Response (combining Product): Before the meeting ends, be sure to summarize action items, owners, and deadlines, and clarify how progress will be tracked afterwards.

In short, thinking through potential risks in advance and preparing response strategies can effectively keep meetings from being interrupted by surprises or derailed, ensuring they run smoothly and achieve their intended goals.

Summary

Through the case-based introduction of the 5P method above, to run a meeting efficiently, the 5P method can effectively keep it from getting out of control. Its core logic is actually this:

“Use structured methods to counter the randomness of human nature”

  • People (the right attendees): Make sure the right people are in the room.
  • Purpose (a clear goal): Be clear about why we are here and where we are going.
  • Process (a clear process): Plan the path well and move forward in an orderly way.
  • Product (the expected output): Leave with results.
  • Pitfall (anticipated risks): Avoid obstacles and arrive smoothly.

In my earlier articles about the four agile meetings, the related practices also reflect the core logic of the 5P method, and I recommend reading them for reference~

item.title: Musk's Weekly Report Mandate and What Weekly Reports Really Are
item.description:
Introduction

One of the hottest topics online these past couple of days has to be Musk’s new DOGE policy — the now-famous “what did you do last week” email requiring every federal employee to send a weekly report listing the five things they did last week, cc’ing their supervisor! Miss it twice in a row and it’s treated as a resignation!

And by now more than 1 million U.S. civil servants have already sent this weekly report! 😂😂😂

As corporate wage slaves, we know this routine all too well — but come to think of it, why do weekly reports even exist?

What Is the Essence of the Weekly (or Daily) Report?

For these U.S. civil servants, writing a weekly report may still be something of a novelty, but for a business-born boss like Musk, weekly reports are a long-standing favorite — he rolled out similar policies at Tesla and Twitter years ago.

So why, from a company’s or a boss’s point of view, do they want to see employees’ weekly reports?

Take a software testing department as an example; the value of a weekly report mainly shows up in the following areas:

  1. Risk control

This should be the part every Leader cares about most in a weekly report. Through weekly reports, you can know the overall progress of the whole project and get a grip on overall quality risks — such as testing delays or insufficient quality exposure. The weekly-report level, unlike a daily report, isn’t overly detailed, so it’s a good input for keeping a handle on the overall status.

  1. Resource optimization

By aggregating and analyzing weekly-report data, a Leader can also grasp how much effort every member is putting in, making it easier to dynamically allocate testing resources.

And this is also the focus of all the attention on Musk’s new policy, because the result the weekly reports point to is that underworked federal employees may get fired 🤪🤪

  1. Decision basis

A weekly report usually also contains some quantitative metrics, such as testing progress, defect data, coverage, escape rate, external support, and other quality data that can be captured or actively reported. These data quantify the current quality state and present it visually, serving as important support for decision-making.

How Should Testers Write a Weekly Report?

So as a test engineer, if we’re going to send a weekly report, what should it usually contain?

Here is a weekly-report example from an employee working on IoT software (a smart band):

I. Weekly Work Summary

 Test execution

 - Completed iterative testing of the heart-rate monitoring module V2.3, covering 10 exercise scenarios, and found 2 critical defects (data delay exceeding the threshold, monitoring failure at low battery).
 - Ran compatibility testing on iOS/Android APP sync; 3 device models (including older ones) showed data loss issues.
 - Regression test pass rate 95%, with the remaining 5% being low-priority UI display issues.

 Defect management

 - Added 15 defects (2 urgent, 5 high priority), closed 8 defects; 3 of the remaining defects require joint fixes with the hardware team.

 Special testing

 - Completed stress testing of the OTA upgrade process; 1 firmware verification failure occurred after simulating 5 consecutive upgrades.
 - In power-consumption testing, the standby power of the sleep-monitoring function exceeded the standard by 20%.

II. Core Issues and Risks

 Blocking issues
 The heart-rate monitoring data delay defect creates a risk of version release delay and needs to be fixed and verified by the development team within 48 hours.

 Resource dependencies
 The hardware team's slow response to sensor issues may affect next week's power-consumption test plan.

III. Next Week's Plan

 - Execute V2.4 feature testing (blood-oxygen monitoring, emergency call).
 - Retest the remaining defects and drive joint debugging with the hardware team.
 - Launch user-scenario stress testing (simulating 1,000 devices uploading data concurrently).

The weekly report above is summarized from two angles — the project and the testing department — and the value it reflects can be summed up in the table below:

Element Value to the Project Value to the Testing Department
Test execution progress Clarifies version quality status and helps the PM assess whether release criteria are met. Quantifies team output, making resource allocation and efficiency optimization easier (e.g., adjusting test case priorities).
Defect distribution and trends Exposes module risks and pushes development to focus on core issues (e.g., a high defect rate in the heart-rate module calls for refactoring). Analyzes root causes of defects (code/design/environment) and drives test case library additions and process improvements (e.g., adding low-battery scenarios).
Risks and dependencies Warns of delay risks and promotes cross-department collaboration (e.g., involving the hardware team). Wins support from upper management (e.g., requesting a longer test cycle or more device resources).
Special test results Validates non-functional requirements (e.g., power consumption, stability), avoiding hard hits to user experience. Accumulates performance baseline data to provide a basis for comparison in later versions (e.g., a power-consumption metric library).
Next week’s plan and goals Aligns with project milestones, keeping testing in sync with development (e.g., the blood-oxygen feature test plan matches the iteration schedule). Clarifies team division of labor, avoiding overlapping or missed tasks.

Summary

So, as an employee, there’s really nothing to resist about weekly reports — it’s just a perfectly normal management practice. For testers, the weekly report is both a “dashboard” for testing work (reflecting quality status in real time) and a “bridge” for cross-department collaboration (driving problem resolution and resource coordination), while also providing data support for optimizing long-term testing strategy.

When it all comes down to it, the goal is still status synchronization

Just like agile stand-ups, and the daily reports that traditional projects may also have, their purpose is actually the same; I’ve covered this in detail in earlier posts, so feel free to refer to those.

item.title: How to Handle Conflicts Between Developers and Testers
item.description:
A reader asked: on a team, developers and testers often run into friction and conflict — how do we avoid such conflicts within the team?

The Origin of Conflict

In a team, conflict between members is actually perfectly normal and very hard to eliminate entirely. The causes vary, but in poor teams conflicts are more likely to arise: mismatched goals and expectations, lack of trust, and poor communication are all common reasons that conflicts arise and even escalate.

Must Conflict Always Be Avoided?

From the standpoint of the project and the product, the friction and conflict between developers and testers isn’t entirely a bad thing. Nor should we take it for granted that conflict must always be avoided.

In many R&D project management practices, the conflict between developers and testers is called constructive conflict — that is, this kind of conflict is constructive for improving product quality, and product quality gets improved through the two sides’ conflict-focused discussions on specific issues.

This idea in fact aligns with how conflict management classifies conflict types.

In conflict management theory, using the two dimensions of how important the matter behind the conflict is and the interpersonal relationship, conflict types can be divided into the following four categories:

  • Constructive conflict: The conflict is task-related, usually aimed at solving a problem, with little impact on the interpersonal relationship between the two sides. This kind of conflict is actually healthy.

  • Destructive conflict: The conflict is also aimed at solving a problem, but it is more intense and damaging to the relationship, affecting friendly cooperation down the line.

  • Dysfunctional conflict: This one is worse — caused purely by the estrangement between the two sides, with little to do with disagreement over the matter itself; you could call it conflict for conflict’s sake.

  • Functional conflict: This is the most common kind, directed at trivial matters and usually showing up as grumbling, joking complaints, and the like.

For the different conflict types, a team should generally encourage constructive conflict, stop destructive conflict promptly, isolate dysfunctional conflict, and tolerate functional conflict while keeping it from accumulating.

The Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Model

For individuals, there is also a theoretical model for how to handle conflict — the Thomas-Kilmann conflict management model:

From two dimensions when facing conflict — your personal assertiveness in solving the problem and your cooperativeness in managing the relationship with the other party — come the following five conflict-handling strategies:

Competing: When an individual is assertive, they can adopt a competing strategy. It creates a win-or-lose situation, where the stronger party forces the other to accept their demands. Win-Lose

Collaborating: This is the best strategy — through cooperation and teamwork, both sides find a win-win path where 1+1>2. Win-Win

Avoiding: Does not solve the problem; a cold treatment that shelves the issue. Lose-Lose

Accommodating: One side voluntarily yields in order to preserve the relationship. Lose-Win

Compromising: Meeting in the middle — both sides give a little and make mutual concessions to reach a middle-ground solution, forming a compromise. Half-Half

Different individuals, when facing conflict, consciously or unconsciously adopt different strategies. Understanding this model helps us assess conflicts more rationally and choose an appropriate way to respond.

How Should a Team Manage Conflict?

For an R&D team, managing conflict well fundamentally comes down to building a strong team culture on the foundation of sound processes and systems, and fostering a transparent, trust-based cooperative relationship and environment.

  • Sound systems. For example, disputes over bugs should have an arbitration mechanism, rather than leaving developers and testers to argue themselves red in the face.

  • Team culture. Testing and development work should not be set against each other; instead, everyone collaborates toward a shared quality goal.

item.title: The 5 Whys Root Cause Analysis Method You Should Know
item.description:
In the field of quality management, an important process for improving quality is discovering problems and solving them. Within this, in the practice of solving problems, a key step is Root Cause Analysis (RCA). There are many RCA methods; commonly used ones include the Fishbone Diagram, the Affinity Diagram, and FMEA (Failure mode and effects analysis), among others.

However, the easiest to apply and the most widely used is probably the 5 Whys root cause analysis method

The Origin of the 5 Whys

The 5 Whys method originated at Toyota and was proposed by Akio Toyoda, the father of Toyota. But its introduction into the mainstream was thanks to Taiichi Ohno, the head of the Toyota Production System.

Toyota’s website has the following passage describing Taiichi Ohno’s advocacy of this method:

Whenever a problem cropped up, Taiichi Ohno encouraged his staff to explore problems first-hand until the root causes were found. “Observe the production floor without preconceptions,” he would advise. “Ask ‘why’ five times about every matter.”

The 5 Whys method is based on the following basic understanding:

“Behind every problem there is a cause, but superficial analysis can only describe the symptoms.” To find the root cause behind a problem, continuous investigation is needed; only by obtaining the root cause can targeted, lasting solutions be adopted so that the problem does not recur.

So the 5 Whys is actually about this: when we encounter a problem, we should not look only at the superficial causes that led to it, but should embrace the spirit of “getting to the bottom of the matter” and dig out its root cause. Only by solving the root cause that gives rise to the problem can we possibly avoid its repeated recurrence.

To take an example from the software industry: during customer acceptance, a fairly serious functional bug was found that affected the final delivery of the product. At this point, the 5 Whys method is used to analyze the root cause:

  1. Why did the customer encounter this problem? According to the technical lead, the testing team had not reported any such issue to the development team

  2. Why was the testing team unable to find the problem? The testing team only performed smoke testing and did not carry out complete regression verification of the functionality

  3. Why did the testing team only perform smoke testing? Because they did not have enough time to perform thorough regression verification of the entire application

  4. Why was there not enough time for thorough regression? Because the version submitted by development for testing was only one day ahead of the final delivery to the customer for acceptance, while thorough functional testing requires at least 3 days.

  5. Why did development submit the build for testing only one day before delivery? Because the implementation of one key feature turned out to be more complex than expected and took more time.

Analyzing up to this point, two root causes are actually discovered:

  • Team members made a serious misestimation of the workload, and development time was underestimated
  • Problems in project management: the build was submitted for testing much later than the testing estimate, sacrificing quality by delivering to the customer without regression. Release-exit control was insufficient.

Therefore, based on the causes identified, improvements are needed in two areas to prevent similar situations from recurring.

  1. Improve the development team’s accuracy in estimating feature implementation, including training, requirements breakdown, and understanding requirements as early as possible.
  2. Improve project management by strengthening test entry/exit control and risk prevention. If the build is submitted late, the delivery time should be postponed accordingly; if a product is released without completing regression, at minimum an exception-release review process must be completed.

Implementation Steps of the 5 Whys

Although the 5 Whys method is very simple, its implementation still needs to follow a certain process of steps:

  1. First, of course, the key members related to the problem need to jointly analyze it. In this step, all relevant roles in the team connected to the problem should be able to participate. Otherwise, the absence of key personnel may cause the analysis to be unable to proceed.

  2. After determining the team members who will participate, it is also necessary to ensure that everyone is fairly clear about the problem: what needs to be analyzed? What background information is there? The team should reach a consensus on the understanding of the problem, rather than entering the Why discussion with different interpretations

  3. During the specific analysis meeting, the facilitator should, through appropriate questioning, gradually help the team unearth the real causes

  4. Of course, the ultimate purpose of analyzing a problem is to solve it, so we also need to discuss corresponding corrective measures for the root cause obtained, in order to prevent similar problems from happening again.

  5. Finally, how effective the implementation of the corrective measures is also needs to be tracked with corresponding actions and time nodes, so as to verify and confirm the effectiveness of the root cause analysis.

Only through such a process is it a complete root cause analysis implementation based on the 5 Whys method.

Considerations When Implementing the 5 Whys

Although the 5 Whys method is simple, in practice it is actually not easy to do well. Here are some key points to note:

A Team Activity

The 5 Whys analysis is a team activity that requires the active participation of people related to the problem. Only when the key roles along the problem analysis path can give effective answers can the validity of the analysis chain be guaranteed

Not an Efficient Method

Although this method is simple to understand, because it is a team activity and is closely tied to whether the various background information about the problem is sufficient, activities including information collection, gathering personnel, and brainstorming in meetings all require an investment of time. It is not an activity that reaches conclusions efficiently or quickly; sometimes it even requires multiple meeting discussions.

The Facilitator’s Experience

Whether the 5 Whys method succeeds depends critically on the role of the meeting facilitator. This role should have a full understanding of the 5 Whys method and be fairly familiar with the problem-related domain, able to guide the team to dig for root causes in the right direction and avoid excessive divergence

Focus on the Issue, Not the Person; Avoid Shifting Blame

Root cause analysis is not about assigning blame; that is, the focus of the meeting is to discover points for future improvement, not to define responsibility for the current problem, so as to avoid turning the analysis meeting into a blame-shifting or finger-pointing session

Focus on Controllable Factors

The root causes obtained from root cause analysis should be controllable factors on which action can be taken, rather than finding force majeure factors that simply cannot be corrected. For example, if there is a shortage of staff, the root cause is that the company is not performing well, and the company’s poor performance is due to an economic downturn.. The conclusion would then fizzle out with nothing being done.

All in all, the 5 Whys analysis method is a simple and practical root cause analysis method, but it is not an efficient one, and its effectiveness is closely related to the concerted effort of team members and the way it is implemented. Only by understanding its internal logic and implementing it selectively according to the team’s actual situation can it truly have the effect it should.
